title.value: On the Conflict between Robustness and Learning in Collaborative Machine Learning
On the Conflict between Robustness and Learning in Collaborative Machine Learning

abstract.value: Collaborative Machine Learning (CML) allows participants to jointly train a machine learning model while keeping their training data private. In many scenarios where CML is seen as the solution to privacy issues, such as health-related applications, safety is also a primary concern. To ensure that CML processes produce models that output correct and reliable decisions even in the presence of potentially untrusted participants, researchers propose to use robust aggregators to filter out malicious contributions that negatively influence the training process. In this paper, we prove that the two prevalent forms of robust aggregators in the literature cannot eliminate the risk of compromise without preventing learning: in order to learn from collaboration, participants must always accept the risk of being the subject of harmful adversarial manipulation. Therefore, these robust aggregators are unsuitable for highstake applications such as health-related or autonomous driving in which errors can result in physical harm. We empirically demonstrate the correctness of our theoretical findings on a selection of existing robust aggregators and relevant applications, including end-to-end results where we show that using existing robust aggregators can lead to an adversary can cause incorrect medical diagnosis or can cause self-driving cars to miss turns. 2171 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

Collaborative Machine Learning (CML) allows partic- ipants to jointly train a machine learning model while keeping their training data private. In many scenarios where CML is seen as the solution to privacy issues, such as health-related applications, safety is also a primary concern. To ensure that CML processes produce models that output correct and reliable decisions even in the presence of potentially untrusted participants , researchers propose to use robust aggregators to filter out malicious contributions that negatively influence the training process. In this paper, we prove that the two prevalent forms of robust aggregators in the literature cannot eliminate the risk of compromise without preventing learning: in order to learn from collaboration, participants must always accept the risk of being the subject of harmful adversarial manipulation. Therefore, these robust aggregators are unsuitable for high- stake applications such as health-related or autonomous driving in which errors can result in physical harm. We empirically demonstrate the correctness of our theoretical findings on a selection of existing robust aggregators and relevant applica- tions, including end-to-end results where we show that using existing robust aggregators can lead to an adversary can cause incorrect medical diagnosis or can cause self-driving cars to miss turns. 1. Introduction Collaborative Machine Learning (CML) allows users to jointly train a machine learning model. The main argument to favor CML rather than centralized learning techniques is privacy: CML enables training of models without the users' data leaving their device. Instead, users share model updates, e.g., gradients or model weights [1]. CML architectures differ in the means they orchestrate the sharing of updates amongst participants, with the main two approaches being server-aided (e.g., Federated Learning [1]), and peer-to-peer (e.g., Decentralized Learning [2]). In many applications where the privacy of CML is typi- cally considered an advantage, the reliability and correctness of a machine-learning model's predictions or classifications, i.e., its robustness, is a critical property. For example in health applications [3]-[12], where incorrect diagnosis can threaten the life of a patient; or in autonomous driving [13]-[19] where wrong predictions threaten the safety of passengers, bystanders, and the environment. Even in fields where robustness is not essential for safety, it may be needed for economic reasons, such as avoiding manipulations that change content visibility in advertisement applications [20] or change credit risk prediction [21]. Lack of robustness may stem from either non-malicious failures, such as users having low-quality data or an unreli- able network connection that prevents them from participat- ing in the network; or from attacks performed by malicious participants whose goal is to influence the behavior of the trained model(s) in some undesirable way. There exist a number of CML-tailored sophisticated functions to improve robustness in the literature [17], [22]-[42] - referred to as robust aggregators [25], byzantine resilient defenses [35], scoring mechanism [27], or even poisoning detectors [43]. Robust aggregators enable participants to evaluate the model updates they receive, and reject those that are deemed detrimental to the final model. Then, participants learn as if there were only honest users in the network. There is a growing number of works in the security liter- ature focusing on robust aggregators, proposing attacks [25], [43]-[47] and mitigations [24]-[26], [43], [46]. These works focus on studying the effectiveness of robust aggregators against a selection of existing attacks, and do not discuss the effectiveness of these defenses against a strategic adversary that adapts to the aggregator. This approach in which re- searchers iterate attacks and defenses towards finding the best robust aggregation function, such as in the search for robust algorithms in the centralized machine-learning literature [48], may overestimate the protection of algorithms, as standard experimental setups can misrepresent robustness [49]. In this paper, we provide the first formalization of the robustness problem in CML and use this characterization to provide insights on the limits of the most prevalent robustness approaches in CML. In both approaches, for honest participants to learn they must always incur a risk of being manipulated. In other words, while a robust aggregator can offer protection against state-of-the-art attacks, it is impossible to prove that there is no attack surface unless participants give up learning. We also show that, if a proof that no adversarial manipulation is possible exists, either collaboration is disabled or participants have large enough local knowledge on the task and in consequence will not learn from collaboration. The impossibility to create a perfectly robust collaborative learning environment makes collaborative learning an unsuitable technique for high stakes 2171 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00249 applications such as healthcare predictions or self-driving. Concretely, we make the following contributions: • We introduce a systematization for robust aggregation techniques in the CML literature. We find that most robust aggregators belong to one of two categories: those that evaluate the robustness of updates based on their distance, e.g., L2-distance to a reference point; and those that evaluate the robustness of updates based on their behavior, e.g., error rate on a test set. • We provide a game-based formalization of the learn- ing and robustness goals in CML. This formalization enables to reason in a principled way about the trade- offs between these two goals. • We prove that there is no robust aggregator that can formally guarantee that users learn from collabora- tion without any risk of manipulation. This makes existing robust aggregators unsuitable for high-stake applications. • We show that if it is possible to prove that there is no risk of manipulation, then participants will not have anything to learn from each other hence do not benefit from collaboration. • We empirically validate our findings on state-of-the- art aggregators, targeting fields where CML has been hailed as the solution to privacy. 2. Robustness in Collaborative Learning Collaborative learning. A Collaborative Machine Learning (CML) system consists of n users who hold private local data. User i holds data Si formed by tuples of samples x and labels y sampled from the domain D = (X , Y). We use the notation (x, y) ∼ D to denote sampling from the domain. We do not assume samples in D follow a specific distribution. Thus, our results apply regardless of how samples are distributed. Users are connected according to a graph G, in which nodes are users and edges represent connections between users. We call this graph topology. A common topology in CML is a star, used in Federated Learning [1], in which all nodes communicate with each other via a central entity. In CML, users initialize their models with common public parameters θ0 and iterate over the following three steps until a stop condition is met: (1) Local training: At the beginning of epoch t, users apply gradient descent on their local model parameters θt using their local data Si, and compute an update ∇t i. (2) Communication: Users share their model update ∇t i with their neighbors- or the server in federated learning. (3) Aggregation: Users (or the server in federated learning) aggregate the updates, e.g., compute their average or their median. Users obtain an updated model θt+1 using the result of their local aggregation. In federated learning, the server updates the global model and sends it to the users. Robustness Adversary: Goal and Capabilities. The primary goal of CML is to enable users to obtain a model which performs better on the learning task than a model trained solely on their local data. In many cases, the application also requires this model to be robust, i.e., the participants must not be able to influence the model in any undesired way. Whereas undesired is subjective and potentially relative to the application, in all cases the goal is to prevent manipulations that result in erroneous model outputs. We evaluate robustness when one, or more, of the participants are adversarial. We only consider as potential adversaries participants that send updates to other partici- pants performing (robust) aggregation, e.g., to the federated server [1] or to peers in decentralized learning [2]. This excludes the scenario where a malicious federated server sends updates to users that accept it without further checks, as in that case, the server can already perform any adversarial manipulation by design. The adversary aims to degrade the performance of the system, either in an untargeted way, e.g., reducing the performance of the model as in a denial of service attack; or in a targeted fashion, e.g., changing the output of some chosen inputs. Following the literature, we assume this adversary to be malicious, i.e., they can send arbitrary model updates to other participants during training e.g., [22, Section 3.2], [27, Section 2] [25, Section 1], [42, Section 2.1], [23, Section 1], [50, Section 3.C]. The precise capabilities of the adversary depend on the CML protocol and the threat model of the application [51]. At a minimum, the adversary, who participates in the training, has knowledge of the training public parameters (model architecture, learning rate) and of the updates it receives from its neighbors. Other capabilities such as the ability to participate in all epochs can vary depending on the CML system. 3. Systematization of Robust Aggregators In CML, the main tool to ensure robustness of the final model is the use of robust aggregatorsduring the training pro- cess. Robust aggregators aim to filter out detrimental updates before aggregation, such that only honest users contribute to training. Robust aggregators rely on an evaluation metric to distinguish benign updates from malicious ones. We use R(∇; D) to refer to the evaluation of the update ∇ on the inputs from the domain D, using the metric R. The output of the evaluation is used in conjunction with a threshold value δ to identify benign updates, e.g., R(∇; D) < δ. A robust aggregator is a concrete instantiation of the metric R and a means to evaluate the exchanged updates, i.e., a metric R represents a definition of robustness. The instantiation of R must have two properties. First, it must capture the difference between benign and malicious updates such that the robust aggregator can effectively reject mali- cious updates: if an update does not influence the model in any way that leads to erroneous results, then R(∇; D) must be below δ. Second, participants must be able to correctly compute R, even when they have access to a limited dataset and limited knowledge on the learning task. Robustness metrics.
